opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really exciting tool, but I'd describe its robustness honestly as "promising but uneven." The basic idea is simple: you find a direction in the model's activation space that corresponds to some concept, say sentiment, refusal, or honesty, and you add or subtract that vector during the forward pass to push the model's behavior. And the striking thing is how often that works with very little effort. A handful of contrastive examples, take the difference in mean activations, and suddenly you can make a model more positive or less likely to refuse. That tells us something real about how these models organize information internally.

But when you look carefully, the robustness picture gets more complicated. First, steering is quite sensitive to where and how strongly you intervene. Pick the wrong layer or scale the vector too much and you don't get a cleaner version of the behavior, you get degraded, incoherent text. So there's often a narrow window where it works well.

Second, the effects can be inconsistent across inputs. A vector that reliably shifts behavior on one distribution of prompts might do very little, or even the opposite, on another. Some of the work my collaborators and I have done on benchmarking interpretability methods, like AxBench, found that when you compare steering head-to-head against simple baselines like prompting or lightweight fine-tuning, steering often doesn't come out on top. Prompting is a surprisingly strong baseline, and that's a humbling result for the field.

Third, there's the question of whether the vector actually captures the concept we think it does. A direction that correlates with "truthfulness" on our examples might really be encoding something more superficial, like formality or confidence of phrasing. So when we say we're editing the model's "thoughts," we should be careful. We're editing activations, and our interpretation of what those activations mean is a hypothesis that needs testing.

So my overall view is that steering vectors are a valuable scientific instrument. They let us run causal experiments on model internals, which is exactly what interpretability needs. But as a practical control mechanism for deployed systems, I don't think they're yet robust enough to replace other methods. The path forward is rigorous evaluation: comparing against strong baselines, testing generalization across distributions, and measuring side effects on capabilities. If we do that work, I think steering and related representation-level interventions can become genuinely reliable tools, but we're not fully there yet.

r001.rationale: The response says excessive steering can produce degraded, incoherent text, but does not state that it harms capabilities unrelated to the intended behavior.

r002.rationale: It describes inconsistent behavioral effects across prompt distributions and recommends measuring capability side effects, but does not say collateral capability effects are unpredictable.

r003.rationale: Fine-tuning is mentioned as a comparison baseline, but the response does not claim it makes collateral capability degradation easier to avoid than steering does.

r004.rationale: The response says steering is not yet robust enough to replace other methods in deployed systems, but does not recommend focusing on methods used in practice if direct editing fails to gain adoption.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, steering vectors are one of those ideas that looks almost too clean on paper. You take activations from a model on contrasting inputs, say "happy" versus "sad" or "honest" versus "deceptive," subtract them, and you get a direction. Add that direction back in during inference and the model's behavior shifts. It feels like you've found a knob for a concept.

My honest assessment is that they work surprisingly well as a demonstration and surprisingly poorly as a dependable tool. Let me unpack both halves of that.

On the positive side, the fact that a linear direction in activation space does anything coherent at all is genuinely informative. It tells us that models represent a lot of high-level features in roughly linear ways, which is a nontrivial empirical claim about how these systems organize information. And in some cases, like refusal behavior, a single direction accounts for a startling amount of what the model does.

But robustness is where it gets uncomfortable. The first problem is that the effect is very sensitive to the steering coefficient. Push too little and nothing happens. Push a bit too much and the model degrades, repeating itself, producing incoherent text, or just collapsing into the concept you're steering toward regardless of context. The usable window is often narrow and it varies across prompts, so a coefficient that works on your evaluation set may fail elsewhere.

The second problem is that the direction is usually not as clean as we hope. When you build a vector from contrasting prompts, you capture the intended concept but also whatever else happened to covary with it in your data. Tone, length, formatting, topic. So you're editing more than you think you are, and the side effects show up in ways your benchmark may not measure.

Third, and this is the one I think matters most for the "editing thoughts" framing, steering a representation is not the same as changing the computation that reads from it. Downstream layers may partially correct for the intervention, or route around it, so what you observe as a behavioral change can be an indirect consequence rather than the direct effect you intended. We've seen interventions that look causal at one layer and essentially get undone a few layers later. That's a problem if you want to make claims about what the model is "thinking."

So where does that leave me? I think steering vectors are an excellent hypothesis-generation and probing tool. They give you fast, cheap evidence that a feature exists and is causally relevant. But treating them as a reliable control mechanism, something you'd deploy to guarantee a model behaves a certain way, is premature. For that you want methods with better specificity, and you want evaluations that actively look for the collateral damage rather than just checking whether the headline behavior moved.

The field is maturing here. People are comparing steering to fine-tuning and prompting on fair footing, measuring unintended effects, and being more careful about whether the linear assumption actually holds for the feature in question. That's the right direction. Early results were a little intoxicating, and now we're in the sober phase where we figure out what these methods actually buy us.

r001.rationale: The response says steering can cause repetition, incoherence, and collateral side effects, but it does not clearly state that strong interventions degrade capabilities unrelated to the intended change.

r002.rationale: It describes side effects and prompt sensitivity, but does not clearly characterize effects on other capabilities as unpredictable.

r003.rationale: Fine-tuning is mentioned only as a method to compare against; the response does not say it makes collateral degradation easier to avoid.

r004.rationale: The response calls steering premature for reliable control, but does not recommend shifting interpretability research toward methods used in practice if direct thought editing fails to gain adoption.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between showing that a steering vector changes behavior and showing that it does so robustly. You can find a direction in a model’s activations that, when you add it, makes the model behave differently on a set of prompts. That’s interesting, but it doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve identified a clean, isolated representation of a particular thought.

The harder question is whether that intervention works across different contexts. Does it still work if you rephrase the prompt, change the topic, or explicitly push the model in the opposite direction? And does it change only the behavior you intended, or does it also hurt the model’s ability to do the task?

There’s also a tradeoff in how strongly you apply the vector. Too little might have no effect; too much might disrupt the model more broadly. So I’d view steering vectors as a promising experimental tool, but I’d be cautious about treating them as a reliable way to edit thoughts. For that, you need evidence that the effect generalizes, that you understand its side effects, and that it holds up under pressure.

r001.rationale: It says applying the vector too strongly might “disrupt the model more broadly” and asks whether it hurts task ability, communicating possible degradation beyond the intended change.

r002.rationale: The response mentions side effects but does not state that their effects on other capabilities are unpredictable.

r003.rationale: It does not compare steering vectors with fine-tuning.

r004.rationale: It does not recommend shifting interpretability research toward methods used in practice if thought editing is not adopted.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between changing a model’s behavior and editing its thoughts. A steering vector changes internal activations, and that can reliably shift some outputs, but it doesn’t necessarily correspond to a clean, isolated concept like a belief or an intention.

Typically, you construct a vector from the difference between activations on contrasting examples, then add it back into the model during inference. That can work quite well in a particular experimental setting. The harder question is whether it keeps working across different prompts, tasks, and steering strengths. You might get the behavior you want on your test set, but also change unrelated behaviors or degrade the model’s capabilities.

So I’d treat steering vectors as useful experimental tools, but I’d be cautious about calling them robust mechanisms for controlling a model. You want evaluations on held-out situations, adversarial prompts, and side effects—not just examples where the intervention looks convincing. Changing an output is a much weaker claim than knowing precisely what internal process you changed.

r001.rationale: It says steering can change unrelated behaviors or degrade the model’s capabilities, and cautions that results may depend on steering strength.

r002.rationale: It warns about side effects but does not say those collateral effects are unpredictable.

r004.rationale: It does not recommend shifting interpretability research toward methods used in practice if direct thought editing is not adopted.
